paragraphs: This paper strengthens theoretical guarantees for policy gradient and natural policy gradient methods, including versions that reduce sampling variability. The central question is whether these methods merely reach a point where local improvement stalls, or can approach the best achievable reward. The analysis considers general smooth policy parameterizations and assumes that the policy’s Fisher information matrix is positive definite.

The key move is to combine two previously separate lines of reasoning. Arguments about reaching stationary points with policy gradients also help analyze natural policy gradients. Conversely, arguments about global convergence for natural policy gradients help establish stronger guarantees for variance-reduced policy gradients. This connection upgrades an existing method’s guarantee to global optimality up to an inherent policy-approximation error.

The authors also establish a lower sample complexity for natural policy gradients and introduce SRVR-NPG, which adds variance reduction to their updates. Its analysis provides global convergence and efficient finite-sample complexity. These findings strengthen what the methods can be guaranteed to achieve under the stated assumptions, while retaining the error associated with the chosen policy representation.
neurips-2020-an-improved-analysis-of-var.tldr: Combining policy-gradient analyses yields stronger conditional convergence guarantees and a variance-reduced natural policy-gradient method.

paragraphs: In reinforcement learning with many goals, choosing what to practice can strongly affect how efficiently an agent learns. Randomly selecting goals may spend effort on tasks the agent already handles or tasks it cannot yet solve. This paper proposes automatically organizing training around the frontier of the agent’s current abilities, where new successes can extend its range of behaviors.

The method adds a goal proposal module that prioritizes uncertainty in the policy’s Q-function, which estimates the value of actions. Specifically, it targets epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty associated with what the learner does not yet know. Value disagreement supplies a way to select goals intended to be neither too easy nor too difficult, turning the agent’s developing knowledge into a training curriculum.

The authors evaluate the approach on 13 robotic tasks with multiple goals and five navigation tasks, reporting gains over current state-of-the-art methods. The results support the usefulness of choosing practice goals adaptively in those settings. The contribution is a simple mechanism for directing experience toward goals that provide a stronger learning signal.
neurips-2020-automatic-curriculum-learni.tldr: An automatic curriculum prioritizes goals with uncertain action values, improving learning across tested robotic and navigation tasks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often benefit when connected nodes have similar features and labels, a property called homophily. This paper examines node classification when that pattern is weak or reversed. Under such heterophily, many popular graph networks fail to generalize well, and models that ignore connections can even perform better. The question is how to make graph structure useful in this setting.

The authors identify three helpful design choices: keep a node’s own representation separate from its neighbors’ representations, consider neighborhoods beyond immediate connections, and combine representations from intermediate stages. They assemble these choices into H2GCN and use it to evaluate their effectiveness. Together, the choices provide ways to retain and combine information without relying solely on similarity between directly connected nodes.

Experiments report accuracy improvements of up to 40% on synthetic networks and 27% on real networks with heterophily over models without these designs. Performance also remains competitive under homophily. These are empirical gains in the studied settings, showing that graph-network design can accommodate relationships between dissimilar nodes.
neurips-2020-beyond-homophily-in-graph-n.tldr: Three architectural choices help graph neural networks classify nodes when connected nodes are dissimilar.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to make deep learning models more resistant to deliberately manipulated inputs. This paper asks whether shaping the model’s learned features can strengthen that defense. It proposes incorporating hypersphere embedding into adversarial training, adding a lightweight representation-learning component to the training procedure.

The embedding regularizes features onto compact manifolds, imposing structure on the space in which the model represents inputs. The authors analyze how this mechanism and adversarial training work together, finding several ways in which their combination benefits robustness. They integrate the component into PGD-AT, ALP, and TRADES, as well as the FreeAT and FastAT training strategies, to investigate its adaptability across different frameworks.

Evaluations use a wide range of adversarial attacks on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. In those experiments, adding hypersphere embedding consistently improves robustness for each tested training framework while requiring little extra computation. The stated finding is therefore both an empirical robustness gain and evidence that the same representation constraint can usefully complement several existing adversarial-training approaches.
neurips-2020-boosting-adversarial-traini.tldr: Hypersphere embedding improves robustness across tested adversarial-training frameworks with little additional computation.

paragraphs: Implicit regularization is the idea that an optimization algorithm tends to select structured solutions that generalize well, even without an explicit penalty enforcing that structure. This paper examines how far that explanation can go for stochastic gradient descent. It works in stochastic convex optimization, a relatively simple setting in which to test claims about optimization and generalization.

The authors first construct an example ruling out a distribution-independent implicit regularizer that governs SGD’s generalization. They then give another learning problem that rules out a broad class of explanations even when the regularizer may depend on the data distribution. This class includes strongly convex regularizers and non-degenerate regularization based on norms.

These constructions challenge the adequacy of explaining generalization solely through a preferred solution structure. Their scope matters: the paper excludes particular broad forms of regularizer-based explanation, rather than showing that implicit bias never exists or never helps. The results reveal substantial obstacles to making implicit regularization a comprehensive account of an algorithm’s generalization performance.
neurips-2020-can-implicit-bias-explain-g.tldr: Counterexamples show that broad classes of implicit regularizers cannot fully explain SGD’s generalization in stochastic convex optimization.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning seeks to improve a policy using a fixed collection of previously recorded experience. It avoids the need to gather fresh interactions during policy optimization, addressing both the expense of data collection and concerns about unsafe exploration. However, the authors observe that many off-policy algorithms perform poorly when restricted to a fixed dataset.

The paper introduces Critic Regularized Regression, or CRR, as an algorithm for learning policies in this offline setting. Its defining approach combines regression-based policy learning with regularization supplied by a critic. This makes the critic part of how learning from the recorded data is guided, rather than relying on additional environment interactions to support policy improvement.

The authors report strong performance across a wide range of benchmark tasks, including tasks with high-dimensional states and actions. CRR significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art offline reinforcement-learning methods in their experiments. These findings support its effectiveness and scalability in the evaluated settings, and show that critic-regularized regression is a promising approach to extracting useful policies from existing experience.
neurips-2020-critic-regularized-regressi.tldr: Critic Regularized Regression learns policies from fixed datasets and outperforms several leading offline RL methods in reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Recognizing whether a hand is making physical contact requires reasoning about its surroundings as well as its appearance. This paper studies joint hand detection and contact-state recognition in unconstrained images. The task is further complicated by the absence of training annotations specifying exactly which object, or part of an object, a hand touches.

The proposed network builds on Mask-RCNN and uses another object detector to locate objects in the scene. Two attention mechanisms connect this contextual information to the detected hands. One pools features from a region enclosing a hand and an object according to their affinity. The other adaptively selects salient features from the plausible contact region. The resulting network, including its attention components, is trainable end to end.

The authors introduce ContactHands, a large-scale dataset annotated with hand locations and contact states, to develop and evaluate the method. Their network achieves approximately 7% relative improvement over a vanilla Mask-RCNN-based contact-recognition baseline. This result supports using object context and selective attention to improve contact-state recognition in the tested images.
neurips-2020-detecting-hands-and-recogni.tldr: A hand-detection network uses object context and two attention mechanisms to improve physical-contact recognition.

paragraphs: This paper studies rankings that must adapt as requests arrive. Each request specifies a set of preferred items and how many of them should appear high in the ranking. The learner must choose its ranking without knowing the next request. Generalized Min-Sum-Set-Cover formalizes this problem, with applications such as ordering products or news according to user preferences.

Directly applying standard no-regret learning methods is computationally inefficient because the space of possible rankings is enormous. The authors instead optimize in the space of doubly stochastic matrices, a reduced representation that supports Online Gradient Descent. A crucial part of the method is computing subgradients efficiently by solving the dual of a configuration linear program.

The algorithm then converts the matrix representation back into rankings using deterministic or randomized rounding, with a small loss in the ranking objective. The paper establishes low regret with polynomial-time computation. Its contribution is to connect an efficiently optimized representation to usable rankings, making online learning tractable for this NP-hard underlying ranking problem.
neurips-2020-efficient-online-learning-o.tldr: Optimizing matrix representations and rounding them into rankings enables polynomial-time, low-regret learning for online preference aggregation.

paragraphs: A scoring function can be evaluated through weighted areas under its ROC curve, allowing evaluation to emphasize selected portions of that curve. This paper studies how accurately such quantities can be estimated from data. It analyzes a plug-in estimator, which substitutes empirical information for the unknown population quantities needed to calculate the weighted area.

The main results are exponential bounds on estimation error. They apply both to a single score function and uniformly across classes of score functions whose complexity can be controlled using Gaussian or Rademacher averages. Uniform control is especially relevant when the same data are used to compare and choose among candidate scoring functions, rather than simply evaluate one fixed choice.

These guarantees provide theoretical justification for learning algorithms that maximize empirical partial area under the curve. They connect an objective measured on available data to its population counterpart under the stated complexity conditions. The paper also demonstrates how advances in nonlinear empirical-process theory can be used to analyze this kind of evaluation and learning objective.
neurips-2020-estimating-weighted-areas-u.tldr: Exponential estimation-error bounds justify learning score functions by maximizing empirical partial area under the ROC curve.

paragraphs: This paper considers a bandit problem in which several arms can be played at each stage and rewards follow Markovian dynamics. It works in the rested-bandit setting and seeks an allocation rule that balances reward collection with learning. The proposed rule combines sample means from every arm with a Kullback-Leibler upper confidence bound computed for just one arm, selected in round-robin order.

For rewards generated by a one-parameter exponential family of Markov chains, the authors prove a finite-time regret bound with logarithmic dependence on the time horizon. The guarantee is asymptotically optimal. Their analysis develops concentration results for Markov chains, including a maximal inequality, and also yields finite-time, asymptotically optimal guarantees for multiple plays with independent rewards from a one-parameter exponential family.

Simulations indicate that updating confidence bounds in round-robin order is substantially more computationally efficient than calculating them for every arm each round. The expected regrets behave similarly in those simulations. Together, the theory and experiments support reducing confidence-bound computation while maintaining strong allocation performance in the specified settings.
neurips-2020-finite-time-analysis-of-rou.tldr: Round-robin confidence-bound updates give asymptotically optimal regret guarantees for specified multi-play bandits while reducing computation in simulations.

paragraphs: An agent’s attempt at one task may earn little reward yet contain useful experience for another. In standard multi-task reinforcement learning, that experience can provide little learning signal when interpreted only through the original task. This paper proposes recovering more of its value by reconsidering which task a recorded behavior is suited to.

Generalized Hindsight uses approximate inverse reinforcement learning to make that reassignment. Given behavior collected while pursuing one task, it identifies another task for which that behavior is better suited. The recorded behavior is then relabeled with the new task and passed to an off-policy reinforcement-learning optimizer. The central change is therefore how existing experience is interpreted and reused across tasks.

The authors compare this approach with standard relabeling techniques on a suite of navigation and manipulation tasks. They report substantially more efficient sample reuse in those experiments. The findings support treating low-reward experience as potentially useful evidence for other objectives, with task selection providing a mechanism for turning that potential into a stronger training signal.
neurips-2020-generalized-hindsight-for-r.tldr: Generalized Hindsight relabels recorded behaviors with better-suited tasks to improve sample reuse in multi-task reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Controlling an unknown linear dynamical system requires learning how it responds while keeping costs low. This paper studies that challenge for general convex costs, measuring regret against the class of strongly stable linear policies. The comparison class is part of the guarantee: performance is assessed relative to those policies over the time horizon.

When cost functions are known, the authors give a polynomial-time algorithm with regret proportional to n cubed times the square root of T, where n combines state and control-input dimensions. The square-root dependence on the horizon is optimal and improves the previous T to the two-thirds bound. The central technique adaptively constructs barycentric spanners in an over-parameterized policy space, using geometry to organize exploration.

The paper also handles bandit feedback, where the available cost information is more limited. Building on stochastic bandit convex optimization, it obtains polynomial-time computation and regret with polynomial dimension dependence and square-root horizon dependence. Both results connect efficient exploration of an unknown system with improved long-run control guarantees.
neurips-2020-geometric-exploration-for-o.tldr: Geometric exploration enables polynomial-time control of unknown linear systems with optimal square-root horizon dependence in regret.

paragraphs: Feature attribution assigns class relevance to locations in an image. For brain imaging, this can help identify features that distinguish a trait, but natural variation and heterogeneous phenotypes make the task difficult. ICAM addresses the challenge of separating class-related image differences from the substantial background variation found across individuals.

The framework creates class-specific attribution maps through image-to-image translation. It uses a VAE-GAN to explicitly disentangle features relevant to the class from background features. This separation is intended to make the resulting maps more interpretable. The model also supports sampling in its latent space, allowing exploration of variation within a phenotype rather than producing only a single fixed account of class relevance.

The authors validate ICAM on two-dimensional and three-dimensional brain-image datasets involving dementia, ageing, and simulated lesion detection. Its attribution maps outperform baseline methods when compared with ground truth. The work thus combines improved attribution in the reported evaluations with a way to investigate phenotype variability, supporting interpretation of discriminative image features without establishing them as causal mechanisms.
neurips-2020-icam-interpretable-classifi.tldr: ICAM separates class-relevant and background brain-image features to produce attribution maps and explore phenotype variation.

paragraphs: Behavior that appears suboptimal may reflect rational decisions under an inaccurate internal model. This paper adopts that hypothesis to infer the beliefs and subjective rewards that best explain an agent’s actions. The problem is especially challenging when the agent receives ambiguous sensory evidence that an outside observer cannot fully access.

The authors extend Inverse Rational Control from discrete settings to continuous actions and continuous nonlinear dynamics. Their method also imputes sensory observations affected by unknown noise private to the agent. They first train an optimal Bayesian agent using deep reinforcement learning across a space of dynamics and subjective-reward models. This enables calculation of how likely an observed action trajectory would be under different candidate internal models.

Gradient ascent then finds model parameters that maximize that likelihood. The authors report successful recovery of the true internal models of rational agents. The result supports an approach to interpreting apparently suboptimal behavior through inferred subjective models, and provides a foundation for studying animal behavior and neural dynamics in complex tasks.
neurips-2020-inverse-rational-control-wi.tldr: Inverse Rational Control infers internal models from actions under partial observation, extending to continuous nonlinear dynamics and private sensory noise.

paragraphs: Following navigation instructions requires connecting language with what an agent sees. Individual objects or direction words are only part of the problem: relationships among scenes, objects, and directional cues also shape what an instruction means. This paper makes those relationships explicit in a graph used to guide the agent’s next action.

The proposed Language and Visual Entity Relationship Graph represents connections between text and vision, along with relationships among visual entities. A message-passing algorithm propagates information between language elements and visual entities. The agent then combines the resulting information to choose an action. This provides a structured way for interpretation of the instruction and perception of the environment to inform each other.

Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art navigation methods. On the unseen test split of Room-to-Room, the method achieves 52% success rate weighted by path length. On Room-for-Room, success weighted by normalized dynamic time warping increases from the previous best of 13% to 34%. These results support the value of explicitly modeling relationships in the evaluated navigation tasks.
neurips-2020-language-and-visual-entity-.tldr: A graph linking language and visual entities improves instruction-following navigation on two reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows model complicated distributions by transforming simpler ones. This paper extends that idea to continuous-time stochastic processes, providing a model for entire evolving time series. Its starting point is a Wiener process, which is transformed through a differential deformation to produce a richer observable process.

The construction preserves useful properties of the base process, including efficient calculation of likelihoods and marginal distributions. Those calculations matter because they make it practical to evaluate observed data and reason about selected times within a series. Treating time continuously also provides a natural way to handle irregular observations and interpolate between them, with the stated setting assuming an independent arrival process.

The authors illustrate the model’s properties on established stochastic processes and evaluate it on synthetic and real-world data. Their experiments demonstrate greater flexibility than variational recurrent neural network and latent ordinary differential equation baselines. The contribution combines expressive time-series modeling with tractable probability calculations, while making irregular observation times part of the continuous-time formulation.
neurips-2020-modeling-continuous-stochas.tldr: Dynamic normalizing flows transform a Wiener process into flexible continuous-time models with efficient likelihoods and interpolation.

paragraphs: Deep learning reconstructions of MR images from sub-sampled Cartesian data can contain visible bands or streaks. These artifacts are particularly pronounced in regions with low signal-to-noise ratios. This paper addresses that specific reconstruction problem by changing the training objective so that the learned reconstruction method is penalized for producing banding structures.

The proposed approach uses an adversarial loss and does not require human annotations identifying the unwanted artifacts. Its practical advantage is that the correction is incorporated during training: reconstruction requires no additional computation or subsequent processing. This makes the method a way to improve the reconstructed image within the existing reconstruction-time computational burden.

In a blind comparison against a strong baseline, board-certified radiologists rank the proposed approach as better at removing banding. The evaluation finds no statistically significant loss of image detail, alongside a substantial reduction in visible artifacts. That finding supports the reported improvement in banding removal; the statistical qualification means it should not be read as proof that every detail is always preserved.
neurips-2020-mri-banding-removal-via-adv.tldr: An annotation-free adversarial loss reduces MRI banding without extra reconstruction-time computation or statistically significant detail loss in expert evaluation.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a three-dimensional object from an image can be more useful when the result consists of a small number of meaningful shape primitives. Yet a collection of parts should also support access to the whole object’s volume and surface. This paper addresses that requirement through a primitive representation that combines implicit and explicit descriptions of shape.

The proposed neural star domain, or NSD, learns primitive shapes within a star domain. The authors show that it is a universal approximator for that domain, while also providing compact, semantic primitives and both forms of shape representation. The approximation claim concerns the star-domain setting; it establishes expressive capacity within the specified shape family.

In image-based reconstruction tasks, the approach outperforms existing methods in semantic capability and in the speed and quality of sampling high-resolution meshes. These findings connect the representation’s structure with practical reconstruction benefits. The overall contribution is a way to represent objects through meaningful parts while retaining access to geometric properties needed to handle those parts collectively.
neurips-2020-neural-star-domain-as-primi.tldr: Neural star domains combine implicit and explicit shape representations, improving semantic reconstruction and high-resolution mesh sampling in reported tasks.

paragraphs: In normal-form games, players independently reducing internal regret can produce play frequencies that converge to correlated equilibrium. This paper asks whether a corresponding result holds in extensive-form games, which represent sequential decisions, simultaneous moves, and private information. These features make correlation more complicated than in the normal-form setting.

The authors introduce trigger regret as an extension of internal regret suited to extensive-form games. They show that when every player has low trigger regret, the empirical frequency of play is close to an extensive-form correlated equilibrium. They then construct an efficient algorithm that reduces trigger regret by decomposing it into local problems at each of a player’s decision points.

The local solutions are assembled into a global strategy, yielding uncoupled no-regret dynamics that converge to the set of extensive-form correlated equilibria. The result applies to n-player general-sum games with perfect recall. It establishes a learning-based route to this equilibrium concept under that assumption, connecting individually controlled local updates to a collective property of repeated play.
neurips-2020-no-regret-learning-dynamics.tldr: Trigger-regret minimization yields efficient uncoupled learning dynamics converging to extensive-form correlated equilibria in games with perfect recall.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates a policy’s expected reward from previously observed data. A single estimate may be insufficient when acting on an overly optimistic assessment would be costly. This paper instead develops upper and lower bounds in a general continuous setting, aiming to characterize a range of rewards consistent with the observations.

The method considers Lipschitz Q-functions, whose values cannot change arbitrarily rapidly as their inputs change. Among all such functions consistent with the observations, it searches for the largest and smallest expected rewards. This turns interval estimation into constrained optimization over a function space. The Lipschitz restriction is central to the construction and to the meaning of the resulting bounds.

The authors introduce Lipschitz value iteration to tighten the interval monotonically and prove that the procedure converges. They describe the method as simple and efficient, and demonstrate practical efficiency across benchmarks. Its contribution is a provably correct bounding procedure within the stated framework, giving policy evaluation an interval-valued result that can be progressively refined.
neurips-2020-off-policy-interval-estimat.tldr: Lipschitz value iteration produces provably correct off-policy reward bounds and progressively tightens them within its function-class framework.

paragraphs: Transfer learning can reduce the data needed for a new task by reusing features learned from earlier tasks. This paper provides statistical guarantees for that idea when each task combines a shared representation with a task-specific function. It asks when training across several tasks can identify a representation that makes subsequent learning cheaper.

For diverse training tasks, the sample complexity of learning the shared representation across t tasks scales as C(H) plus t times C(F). Here, C(H) measures representation-class complexity and C(F) measures task-specific function complexity. The representation does not need to be directly observed. Once it has been estimated accurately, learning a new task requires sample complexity scaling only with C(F).

The guarantees depend on a new general notion of task diversity and a chain rule for Gaussian complexities. The authors demonstrate the framework’s usefulness in several models. The central implication is conditional: sufficiently diverse tasks can spread the cost of learning shared features across training tasks, leaving a smaller task-specific learning burden for a new task.
neurips-2020-on-the-theory-of-transfer-l.tldr: Statistical guarantees show how diverse training tasks can support reusable representations that reduce new-task sample complexity.

paragraphs: This paper studies the eigenvalue distributions of two matrices associated with multilayer feedforward networks: the conjugate kernel and the neural tangent kernel. It considers a regime in which network width grows linearly with the number of samples. The analysis assumes randomly initialized weights and inputs satisfying a form of approximate pairwise orthogonality.

Under these conditions, the eigenvalue distributions converge to deterministic limits. For the conjugate kernel, the limit is obtained by repeatedly applying the Marcenko-Pastur map across hidden layers. For the neural tangent kernel, the limiting distribution matches that of a linear combination of conjugate-kernel matrices from different layers. Recursive fixed-point equations describe this second limit.

The authors compare their asymptotic predictions with observed spectra for synthetic data and CIFAR-10 training data, finding agreement. They also run a small simulation examining how spectra evolve during training. The main theoretical contribution concerns initialization in the specified asymptotic regime, while the experiments show how its predictions relate to observed finite-network spectra and offer an initial look at training dynamics.
neurips-2020-spectra-of-the-conjugate-ke.tldr: Under stated initialization and input assumptions, neural-network kernel spectra converge to deterministic limits when width scales linearly with sample size.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines models trained locally by different clients. Because clients have different datasets and computation speeds, they may perform very different numbers of updates before their models are aggregated. This paper shows that naive weighted averaging can then create objective inconsistency: the global model approaches a stationary point of an objective that differs from the intended one.

The mismatch can be arbitrarily large, so making progress on the aggregated objective does not necessarily mean solving the intended learning problem. The authors develop a general convergence-analysis framework covering heterogeneous federated optimization methods, including FedAvg and FedProx. It explains both the bias in the resulting solution and the slowdown associated with objective inconsistency.

Using that analysis, the paper introduces FedNova, a normalized averaging method that eliminates the objective inconsistency while preserving fast error convergence. The contribution links a specific failure mechanism to an aggregation correction. It clarifies why unequal amounts of local computation affect what is optimized, and provides a method designed to align aggregation with the true objective.
neurips-2020-tackling-the-objective-inco.tldr: FedNova normalizes federated averaging to eliminate objective mismatch caused by unequal local updates while retaining fast error convergence.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning research needs environments that challenge agents without making experience prohibitively expensive to collect. The NetHack Learning Environment addresses that combination using the terminal-based roguelike game NetHack. It provides a scalable, procedurally generated, stochastic environment with a rich set of challenges for learning agents.

The authors argue that the game’s complexity can support sustained research on exploration, planning, skill acquisition, and language-conditioned reinforcement learning. Its simulation also substantially reduces the computational resources required to gather large amounts of experience. The paper compares the environment and its task suite with alternatives and discusses its suitability for testing robustness and systematic generalization.

Experiments use a distributed deep reinforcement-learning baseline and Random Network Distillation exploration, demonstrating success in early stages of the game. Qualitative analyses examine several trained agents. Those findings establish initial learning progress rather than mastery of the entire environment. The contribution is an open-source research platform that combines challenging behavior with efficient experience generation, along with baseline results showing how agents begin to engage with it.
neurips-2020-the-nethack-learning-enviro.tldr: The NetHack Learning Environment offers complex, efficient RL tasks, with baseline agents demonstrating progress in the game’s early stages.

paragraphs: The information bottleneck objective expresses a trade-off between task performance and robustness. Applying it to normalizing flows creates an apparent conflict: flows use invertible networks that preserve information, whereas a bottleneck involves discarding information. This paper develops IB-INNs, conditional normalizing flows trained with an information-bottleneck objective, to reconcile those requirements.

The method introduces a small, controlled amount of information loss. This permits an asymptotically exact formulation of the bottleneck while preserving the network’s ability to generate data. The authors then investigate these models as generative classifiers, a setting where uncertainty estimation and out-of-distribution detection are attractive capabilities but traditional approaches suffer in classification accuracy.

Experiments show that the bottleneck trade-off parameter controls a mixture of generative capabilities and classification accuracy close to that of standard classifiers. In this mixed regime, uncertainty estimates compare favorably with conventional generative and discriminative classifiers. The findings support using a single training trade-off to retain generation while obtaining competitive classification and useful uncertainty estimates in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2020-training-normalizing-flows-.tldr: Controlled information loss lets invertible generative models use an information bottleneck to balance generation, classification accuracy, and uncertainty estimation.
